title: Health rebate shift reignites states-feds fight
full_text:
State and territory ministers will demand more cash from the commonwealth if the federal government’s cuts to private health insurance rebates for elderly Australians force more patients into their public health systems, with tensions reigniting just months after a $25bn hospital funding deal was finally struck.
As ministers met with federal counterpart Mark Butler in Sydney on Friday, Ageing Australia warned aged-care providers are already dumping plans to build thousands of new beds, after the commonwealth’s announcement this week that the Australian National Aged Care Classification price would be raised by 2.55 per cent.
The increase has been branded by critics as a real-term cut compared to inflation.
While state and territory ministers entered the meeting furious over bed block in their public hospitals caused by elderly Australians waiting for aged-care placements, the commonwealth’s proposed changes to health insurance rebates has become another contentious issue between the levels of government.
NSW Health Minister Ryan Park, who chaired the meeting, said jurisdictions would pressure their federal counterparts for extra funding if the changes diverted more elderly Australians into public health systems.
“I think all of us have made it clear to Minister Butler … that if there a re going to be additional costs put on state and territories because of this policy change, then we would expect to have a discussion with the commonwealth about financially footing the bill around that,” Mr Park said.
“We just cannot have a situation where we have any more pressure put on our states’ and territories’ public hospitals at the moment … with overall volume rising, whilst we’ve still got long-stay patients stuck in our hospitals, we can’t afford to have anything added in.” Mr Park said modelling showed insurance changes could shift up to $100m worth of pressure on to the NSW public system alone, although Mr Butler later contested the modelling jurisdictions were relying on.
Mr Butler said the commonwealth had made “eye-watering” investments in aged care, but that was being challenged by “unprecedented” demand driven by ageing Baby Boomers.
He also rebuked his counterparts for their concerns over the insurance changes, claiming they were relying on modelling from the insurance industry, which he said showed more Australians would be forced into the public health system, compared to the commonwealth’s own modelling.
“So I say to my state minister colleagues, have a look at the government’s modelling, have a look at the independent modelling done by the University of Melbourne, rather than simply accepting arguments that in the past have been shown to be self-serving from the insurance industry,” he said.
Peak body Ageing Australia on Friday also revealed aged-care providers have already slashed plans to build 2000 new aged-care beds following Wednesday’s announcement that the Australian National Aged Care Classification price would increase by 2.55 per cent.
Ageing Australia CEO Tom Symondson said multiple providers had called him since Wednesday’s announcement saying they had shelved plans to build new beds and facilities due to the paltry increase of the ANACC, which he said was swamped by surging inflation, wages and food costs.
“Beds that had just about been made viable by some of the changes have now tipped back into not being financially viable,” he said.
“We’ve got provider after provider contacting us, distraught, (saying they’re shelving) 100 beds here, 80 beds there.
“The sector wants to help, we want to build beds … the government just needs to stop making it impossible for us and we’ll solve this problem for them.” Chris Mamarelis, CEO of not-for-profit aged-care provider Whiddon, said the ANACC had contributed to the shelving of plans to build 160 new aged-care beds in southwest Sydney.
“We’re pushing plans aside for further residential aged care development in southwest Sydney where it’s desperately needed, because it’s not viable,” he said. “The lack of existing viability is now being compounded even further by the most recent ANACC announcement this week, it sends us backwards.”
